lines.text: Flip a coin. That’s your odds of your state legislative race actually being contested in Massachusetts.
Since 2014, 51% of races in this state — more than half — have had just ONE name on the ballot. No opponent. No debate. No choice.
Massachusetts ranks dead last in the country for electoral competitiveness.
That’s not democracy, that’s your leaders being chosen for you.
And it’s not because good candidates don’t exist — it’s because the system makes it nearly impossible for a challenger to even get on the ballot in the first place.
So every two years, the same seats go back to the same people, and nobody has to explain a single vote. Voters show up… to rubber-stamp a decision that was already made for them.
More than half of Massachusetts races since 2014 have been completely uncontested. Think about that.
When there’s only one name on the ballot, there’s no debate, no comparison, and no reason for anyone to earn your vote.
Question 3 would put every candidate on one primary ballot, and the top finishers would move on to November. Every voter, in every party or none, gets a say.
That means real campaigns in the fall, with candidates who have to knock on doors, show up to debates, and explain where they stand.
It’s a simple change. More choices on the ballot, and representatives who have to answer to all of us.
Vote yes on Question 3.
In most Massachusetts races, there’s no competition — one candidate, one party, no choice.
Why does that matter? Think about the only coffee shop in town. If nobody else can open across the street, prices go up and service goes down. Nobody has to try.
Politics works the same way. When politicians don’t have to compete, they don’t have to listen.
Since 2014, more than half of the races for the State House and Senate have had just one name on the ballot.
Question 3 changes the rules. Every candidate runs in one primary, and the top two finishers face off in November.
Two real choices in the fall means every vote has to be earned. That’s how you get representatives who actually listen.
Here’s a line from a national poll this January: open primaries would produce better candidates — candidates who appeal to a majority of voters, not just their base.
Seventy-three percent of voters agreed. Democrats, Republicans and independents — majorities of all three.

Now look at Massachusetts. In the last decade, nearly two-thirds of our state legislative races had exactly one name on the November ballot. Nobody had to appeal to a majority. Nobody had to appeal to anyone.
Question 3 is the fix: one primary, every candidate on it, every voter gets a ballot, and the top finishers go to November.
If you think candidates should have to win over a majority, this is how you make them.
Vote yes on Question 3.
Quick quiz. What’s the biggest political party in Massachusetts?
It’s not the Democrats — they’re twenty-four percent of registered voters. It’s not the Republicans — eight percent. It’s unenrolled: two out of every three of us belong to no party at all.
But primaries are still run party by party. You pick one ballot, you get a say in that one race — and by November, most races here have just one name left anyway.
Question 3 ends the sorting. One primary, every candidate on it, every voter gets the same ballot, and the top finishers move on.
Two-thirds of this state never joined a party. The election should work for them too.
Vote yes on 3.
Quick question: who ran against your state rep in the last election?
If you can’t remember, here’s why. In 2022, one hundred six of the one hundred sixty Massachusetts House districts had exactly one name on the ballot. Two out of three.
Mine was one of them. No debate. No one knocking on my door. The election was over before it started.
Question 3 would change that: every candidate in one primary, every voter voting, and the top finishers facing off in November. Even a safe seat would have to be defended out loud.
Look up your district. If nobody ran against your rep either, now you know what to do about it.
Vote yes on Question 3.
The strongest argument against Question 3 is that it could put two candidates from the same party on the November ballot.
That’s true. It can.

Here’s what’s also true: in Massachusetts right now, nearly two-thirds of legislative races put ONE candidate on the November ballot. We skipped the two-of-the-same-party problem and went straight to none.
Washington has used a top-two primary since 2008, California since 2012. Hundreds of elections. It’s not an experiment anymore — it’s just how they vote.
And when two candidates from one party do face off, everyone else finally gets a say in which one wins.
Two names on every ballot, picked by everybody, beats one name picked for you.
Vote yes on Question 3.
